summary: Short post after FLIPR's launch. It covers operations: near-daily updates, usually after morning or early-evening poll releases; primary winners replacing pre-primary candidate guesses, which come from polls and prediction markets. It restates Silver's argument against using prediction markets as model inputs, and criticizes markets' overconfidence in the 2026 Michigan and Wisconsin Democratic primaries. It gives empirical primary-poll error figures: an average 9-point error on the margin for presidential primaries, a 22-point 95 percent margin of error, and possibly 25-30 points for down-ballot primaries.

findings.statement: Before a state's primary, FLIPR uses 'educated guesses' of each party's nominee, based simply on polls and prediction markets with no attempt at value-added prediction, and replaces them with actual winners after the primary. FLIPR is a general-election model, not a primary model.
findings.evidence_quote: We usually just go by polls and prediction markets and these very much aren’t intended as any sort of value-added prediction; FLIPR is a general election model, not a primary model.

findings.statement: FLIPR is updated almost every day with no fixed time, usually around 9-11 AM or 5-6 PM Eastern following poll release patterns, and multiple updates per day are avoided unless there is big news.
findings.rationale: Polls tend to come out early morning or late afternoon.
findings.evidence_quote: We do try to avoid multiple updates in a day unless there’s really big news.

findings.statement: FLIPR does not use prediction market prices as inputs; Silver strongly objects to doing so in election models, for the reasons given in SBSQ #30: independence, recursivity, collinearity and markets being a moving target.
findings.evidence_quote: I voiced a strong objection to using prediction markets as inputs in forecasting models. FLIPR does not do this

findings.statement: Historically, presidential primary polls have an average error of 9 points on the margin between the top two finishers, which implies a 95 percent margin of error of about 22 points. Silver suspects down-ballot primaries, with lower turnout, have effective margins of error of 25 to 30 points.
findings.rationale: Lower turnout makes primaries harder to poll.
findings.evidence_quote: Historically, the average error of presidential primary polls is 9 points in predicting the margin between the top two finishers

findings.statement: For a model or market to be well calibrated, 5 percent chances must happen about 5 percent of the time, not zero; quantifying uncertainty is described as most of the work in a model like FLIPR.
findings.evidence_quote: for a model or a market to be well-calibrated, 5 percent chances are supposed to happen 5 percent of the time, not zero percent.

findings.statement: Silver looks at prediction markets daily and finds them useful for diagnosing potential problems with a model and for honing in on outcomes as election-night results arrive, but not as a source of information beyond what is public, except sometimes for the wrong reason (insider trading).
findings.evidence_quote: they’re very useful, for instance, in diagnosing potential problems with your model

findings.statement: In the 2026 Wisconsin Democratic governor primary, three candidates dropped out within weeks for reasons unrelated to frontrunner Francesca Hong's strength, and one later re-entered and won. Silver argues such fluid fields warrant extra caution beyond what the polls imply.
findings.evidence_quote: Wisconsin, in particular, ought to have been a case where traders were more cautious

references.description: SBSQ #30 on prediction markets in models
Long-term studies of prediction market calibration
